strengths: BiAlign presents a coherent and relevant extension to knowledge distillation: aligning teacher–student preferences over demonstration subsets alongside token-level output distributions. The method adds no inference-time overhead.

Table 1 reports consistent improvements across five benchmarks. Compared with Output-Align, average performance increases from 29.2 to 30.2 with the 13B teacher and from 30.0 to 31.7 with the 70B teacher. Experiments with a larger student and the Phi family broaden the empirical support.

The computational controls are valuable. Both subset-augmented Output-Align and reduced-epoch BiAlign comparisons support benefits beyond additional training computation or exposure to more contexts. Numerous ablations examine sampling, demonstration counts, loss weights, and training duration.

The equations, pseudocode, public model and dataset choices, and basic hyperparameters make the core approach understandable and implementable. Improved preference agreement on 500 held-out MMLU examples also supports the intended effect of the ranking objective.
weaknesses: Statistical reliability is insufficiently characterized: run counts, random seeds, and uncertainty estimates are absent despite several small gains. HumanEval improvements represent only one or two additional solved problems out of 164. Moreover, the reported 14.2% and 13.2% baseline scores cannot arise from a single accuracy calculation over 164 problems, so the evaluation or aggregation protocol needs clarification.

Exact replication remains under-specified. The paper provides no implementation link or constructed training examples, and omits important details about CrossFit sampling and templates, evaluation prompts and scoring, optimizer configuration, and QLoRA settings. Table 9 reports GSM8K's full dataset size rather than identifying the evaluated split and count.

The evidence supports improved performance under the evaluated prompting settings more strongly than a specific improvement in learning from demonstrations. Preference agreement does not establish that the performance gains arise from better demonstration use. Comparisons across zero-shot and few-shot settings on the same tasks, and controls holding subset size fixed, would strengthen this interpretation. Cross-dataset relative gains and selected reasoning examples also provide limited support for the claim of preferential improvement on more complex reasoning.

The broader superiority and novelty claims exceed the comparisons. Output-Align is a useful direct baseline, but other cited distillation approaches are not evaluated. The simpler ranking formulation in Table 8 slightly exceeds the proposed formulation, leaving its particular design insufficiently justified. These limitations constrain the main-conference case; the consistent empirical gains and meaningful controls nevertheless support a Findings recommendation.
